summary: Rebecca learns that Esau intends to kill Jacob and persuades Isaac to send Jacob to her relatives for a wife. After Isaac reassures the grieving Rebecca, Jacob journeys alone and dreams at Bethel of a ladder, angels, and God's promise of land, descendants, protection, and return; he marks the place and vows a tenth of what he receives.
whyItMatters: Flight from a family crisis becomes a journey under a renewed ancestral promise. Bethel and Jacob's vow establish obligations that his later return will revisit.

context.author: In the book's Sinai frame an angel recounts this material to Moses. That narrative speaker is distinct from the historical author, whom this chapter does not identify.
context.audience: Moses receives the account inside the story for Israel and its descendants. The historical work addresses Jewish concerns about covenant, inherited stories, and observance; a specific first community is uncertain.
context.date: The narrative uses a chronology counted from creation within its Sinai revelation frame. The historical work is usually placed in the second century BCE; an exact composition date is not established.
context.setting: Isaac and Rebecca's household, followed by Jacob's solitary overnight stop at Luz, identified as Bethel, on the road to Haran.
context.literaryForm: Departure narrative, consoling speech, divine dream, and a vow marking a sacred place.

before.text: Esau has resolved to kill Jacob after losing Isaac's blessing. That threat makes Jacob's departure urgent.

here.text: The chapter moves from a mother's effort to prevent fratricide to God's promise to accompany Jacob beyond his father's household.

after.text: Jacob reaches Laban and works for Rachel, but Laban gives Leah first, beginning a new period of household conflict.

outline.heading: Rebecca prevents a fatal confrontation
outline.note: Jacob first threatens resistance and then refuses to leave without Isaac’s consent.

outline.heading: Isaac sends Jacob to seek a wife
outline.note: Marriage within the maternal family supplies the stated reason for departure and renewed blessing.

outline.heading: Isaac comforts Rebecca
outline.note: Rebecca grieves, and Isaac predicts Jacob’s safe return.

outline.heading: The dream at Bethel
outline.note: A solitary night becomes the setting for the divine promise.

outline.heading: A pillar and a vow
outline.note: Jacob names the place, anoints the stone, and pledges a tenth.

keyVerses.text: But she said unto him: 'Let me not be bereft of both my sons on one day.'
keyVerses.why: Rebecca names the risk of losing both sons and acts to interrupt the threatened violence.

keyVerses.text: And behold, I will be with thee, and will keep thee whithersoever thou goest, and I will bring thee again into this land in peace; for I will not leave thee until I do everything that I told thee of.'
keyVerses.why: The divine speech promises presence and return throughout Jacob’s displacement.

keyVerses.text: And Jacob vowed a vow unto the Lord, saying: 'If the Lord will be with me, and will keep me in this way that I go, and give me bread to eat and raiment to put on, so that I come again to my father's house in peace, then shall the Lord be my God, and this stone which I have set up as a pillar for a sign in this place, shall be the Lord's house, and of all that thou givest me, I shall give the tenth to thee, my God.'
keyVerses.why: Jacob’s vow links protection, food, clothing, return, sacred place, and a tenth.

questions.question: Why does Jacob initially refuse to flee?
questions.answer: He first says he could kill Esau if attacked, then objects that leaving his aged father without permission could bring a curse. Rebecca therefore obtains Isaac's explicit authorization for the journey.

questions.question: Why is finding a wife part of the departure?
questions.answer: Rebecca raises her distress over Esau's Canaanite wives, and Isaac tells Jacob to marry a daughter of Laban. The marriage instruction gives the journey a family purpose alongside the danger already disclosed to the reader.

questions.question: How should the blanket claim that Canaanite daughters are evil be read?
questions.answer: It is Rebecca's sweeping judgment within this story, supporting the book's boundary around marriage. It does not establish the moral character of every member of an ancient population or justify ethnic judgments about people today.

questions.question: What reassures Rebecca after Jacob leaves?
questions.answer: Isaac says God will preserve Jacob, prosper his journey, and bring him home in peace. The reassurance is especially striking because Rebecca herself arranged the departure and still suffers grief at the separation.

questions.question: What is the ladder doing in the dream?
questions.answer: It connects earth and heaven while angels ascend and descend and the Lord speaks. The dream presents the place as a meeting of the earthly journey and divine presence; it gives no instructions for constructing such a ladder.

questions.question: What does “Bethel” mean within this scene?
questions.answer: Jacob calls the place the house of God and the gate of heaven, then names it Bethel, formerly Luz. The name functions as a memorial to the encounter, marked by the stone he sets upright and anoints.

questions.question: Is Jacob promising a payment in advance for protection?
questions.answer: His vow is conditional in its wording: if God keeps and provides for him and returns him safely, he will acknowledge God and give a tenth. The narrative first presents God's promise and then Jacob's response, without explaining the vow as a price that purchases protection.

glossary.def: A solemn promise Jacob makes concerning allegiance, a holy place, and a tenth of his possessions.
The stone Jacob sets upright and anoints as a sign of the encounter at Bethel.
One part in ten of what Jacob receives, pledged in his vow.
